A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AMBER research, with matching methods, datasets, and retained experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite added material and renumbering in v2.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and Appendices H–I report original mesh-generation experiments, baseline comparisons, Poisson simulation-error evaluations, and ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds joint-training comparisons, runtime measurements, downstream-error evaluations, and expanded sensitivity studies.

M1.justification: The core sizing-field prediction, loss, hierarchy, replay buffer, and iterative generation procedure remain unchanged. Section 4 adds AMBER (Mixed), which introduces one-hot task identifiers and zeros for unavailable task-specific features to support joint training.

E1.justification: Both versions use Poisson, Laplace, Airfoil, Beam, Console, and Mold with the same represented domains and mesh-generation tasks. Joint training and expanded analyses reuse these datasets; they introduce no new domain or held-out-task evaluation.

E2.justification: The published Image, GraphMesh, and ASMR baselines and existing variants are retained. V2 adds the AMBER (Mixed) comparison in Table 1 and includes the expert heuristic alongside supervised methods in the new error-indicator comparison in Table 5. This is a limited expansion of comparisons, without replacing baseline implementations.

E3.justification: V2 adds joint training on 60 meshes from three datasets, runtime-versus-error evaluation, and error-indicator comparisons across supervised methods. It also introduces two- and four-generation-step configurations and additional training-size settings, including 10 and 15 samples. These substantially extend the evaluation design while retaining the original main-experiment settings.

E4.justification: New analyses examine downstream-error consistency with mesh-similarity metrics (H.2), runtime and component costs (H.3), and sensitivity to generation-step count (H.7). Data-efficiency analysis expands from Laplace alone to Laplace, Beam, and Console. Table 1 additionally tests whether joint training can replace separate models.

E5.justification: Both versions report five random seeds, mean and twice-standard-error bars in Figure 3, and individual-seed Pareto results. V2's checklist explicitly summarizes these conventions. The added results do not establish increased replication, new significance testing, or a changed uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results while retaining the main benchmark plots. Table 1 reports separate versus mixed-training scores, including 0.224 versus 0.226 on Poisson (hard). Table 5 adds error norms with element counts; Figure 8 and Table 6 add runtime results, including reported speedups exceeding 10 times the expert heuristic above 30,000 elements. Expanded data-size and generation-step results are also new.

T1.justification: Appendix B retains the same one-dimensional convergence theorem, perfect-prediction assumptions, and inductive proof. The method, PDE, metric, and ablation equations remain mathematically unchanged; added notation clarifications do not introduce new formal results.

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions remain essentially unchanged. The introduction adds an explicit claim that AMBER is faster and scales better than classical iterative error-estimation methods. The conclusion replaces the separate-model limitation with an experimentally supported statement about training one model across multiple datasets.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the new error-indicator comparisons as support for DCD as a simulation-error proxy and explains runtime dominance through mesh-generation costs relative to graph operations. Joint-training results motivate broader applicability. The limitations concerning anisotropy and untested real-world simulation accuracy remain.

D1.justification: V2 explicitly clarifies that the MPN is shared across generation steps and documents the mixed model's task encoding, missing-feature handling, and shared replay buffer. It adds component timings and changes the resource footnote from a repository link to a project-page access point. Existing hardware and core hyperparameters remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 replaces the monitor-function-based distinction from mesh-movement methods with a distinction concerning fixed starting resolution versus changing element counts. The McRae, Cotter, and Budd (2018) reference is removed; the remaining cited works are retained.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and most existing prose remain intact. V2 adds focused runtime and joint-training discussion, revises related-work and limitations passages, clarifies method wording, and expands Appendix H. It also inserts a NeurIPS checklist and updates the conference footer, without wholesale rewriting or reorganization.

P2.justification: V2 adds joint-training, downstream-error, and runtime tables (Tables 1, 5, and 6), runtime plots (Figure 8), and generation-step plots (Figure 12). V1's combined Figure 10 becomes an expanded data-efficiency figure and a separate image-ablation figure. Most other visualizations are retained and renumbered, but the new displays substantially expand the presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 usefully strengthens an already extensive evaluation with measured inference costs, wider downstream-error comparisons, and joint-training evidence addressing v1's separate-model limitation. Expanded data-size and generation-step studies also better support practical choices. These gains remain bounded: joint training evaluates represented tasks, and industrial simulation accuracy remains untested. The revision improves empirical support without materially changing the central method or established benchmark findings.
